Seven research-based practices offer steps for evaluating and introducing AI tools with a focus on trust, human oversight, job design and workers’ well-being

Washington — As organizations introduce artificial intelligence (AI) tools to their workforce, people may be left to navigate unclear policies, conflicting expectations and new questions about trust and acceptable AI use in the workplace.

A new guide released by the American Psychological Association outlines what organizations should consider when introducing AI into people’s work.

Created for organizations seeking to adopt AI responsibly while also supporting employees and improving how work is designed, Deploying AI Into Workplaces: What Leaders Need to Know offers seven best practices based on established psychological research and emerging evidence about AI. These range from matching safeguards to the stakes of potential errors to ensuring that AI is introduced through a fair process.

“The rapidly growing use of AI at work is creating new behaviors and social judgments while raising questions about trust, all of which are fundamentally questions of psychology. Did you use AI to write your emails today? Am I supposed to think more or less of you if you did?” said APA CEO Arthur C. Evans Jr., PhD. “Psychological science can help organizations understand not just what AI tools can do, but how their use affects trust, decision-making and employee well-being. APA’s new guide gives leaders a practical framework for introducing AI thoughtfully, with people at the center of the process.”

The share of workers reporting pressure from their employers to use AI at work is rising. Yet, according to APA’s 2026 Work in America Survey released earlier this year, less than 40% of workers for whom this question applied reported knowing whether their employer had an official policy about acceptable AI use.

To address the adoption-policy mismatch, APA’s new guide offers a practical checklist with seven ways to help organizations introduce, use and evaluate AI tools responsibly. It also offers examples of what effective AI tool implementation can look like, as well as identifies the red flags to watch out for. Rather than providing universal instructions or telling organizations whether or not to use AI tools, the guide is designed to help organizations that choose to introduce these tools do so thoughtfully.

Developed with input from an advisory panel of experts in human-technology interaction and clinical, social, legal, cognitive and industrial-organizational psychology, the guide’s suggested practices include:

“Purchasing an AI tool and telling people to use it without further direction is not a sound strategy,” said Dennis P. Stolle, JD, PhD, executive lead psychologist for applied psychology at APA. “Organizations need to invest in the people who will work with the technology, not just the technology itself. That means giving workers the information they need to judge where AI tools are reliable and where they are not, making sure human oversight is meaningful and rethinking how jobs are designed.”
